questions.question:
**The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.**

We bought / two dozens / mangoes from / the market.
questions.solution:
The erroneous art is **'two dozens'.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The given sentence is grammatically incorrect.
 
• Here,** 'two dozen' **should be used instead of** 'two dozens'.**
 
• We never write **‘dozens’ **if we are using a numerical amount like *two, three, etc. *before it.
 
 
• *For example, **‘two dozens of bananas’ **is incorrect but **‘three dozen of mangoes’ **is correct. *
 
 
 
• Similarly, the given sentence has ‘**two**’ as** a numerical value.**
 
• Thus, the correct answer is** Option 4.**

 

**Correct Sentence:__** *We bought **two dozen** mangoes from the market.*

questions.question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.

You shall repented tomorrow for your misdeeds.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 3)**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In the given sentence, the phrase 'shall repented' is incorrect.
 
• The correct form should be **'shall repent'** to match the future tense.
 
• The word** 'shall'** is a modal verb that should be followed by the **base form of the main ver**b, which is 'repent' in this case.
 
 
• **Example:** *You ** shall repent ***tomorrow for your misdeeds.
 
 

Hence the correct statement is* **You shall repent tomorrow for your misdeeds**.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Modal verbs like **shall, will, can, could, may, might, must, ought to, should, would** are always followed by the **base form of the main verb**.

 
 
• **Example:** *She **can swim** very well.*

questions.question:
**The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.**

Raju was / a little boy / who were born / in a poor family.
questions.solution:
The erroneous part of the sentence is: **who were born**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The error here lies in the subject-verb agreement.
 
• The basic rule states that a singular subject takes a singular verb while a plural subject takes a plural verb.
 
• Raju is a third-person singular subject.
 
• In the first case "was" is used for a singular subject which is perfectly fine.
 
• We use "who" in the sentence to replace the noun. ('Raju' in this sentence)
 
• So, we must use "was" (singular verb) in the second case.

Therefore, the correct answer is **option 4**, which contains an error.

**Corrected sentence:** *Raju was a little boy who **was **born in a poor family.*

questions.question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.

I wish / I am / the Principal / of the school!
questions.solution:
The erroneous part is **'I am'. **

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The given sentence is an example of **subjunctive mood.**
 
• The **subjunctive mood** is the verb form used to explore a hypothetical situation (e.g., "If I were you") or to express a wish, a demand, or a suggestion (e.g., "I demand he be present").
 
• **I am **is the normal present tense verb form. It cannot be used for the subjunctive mood. 
 
• Hence, **option 3 **is the correct answer. 
 
• The sentence can be corrected by using **I were.**

**Correct sentence__ - ***I wish / **I were** / the Principal / of the school!*

questions.question:

There’s an quiet street down the left that you can use for your dance practice.
questions.solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The primary issue in the sentence is the use of the article "**an**" before the term "**quiet street**."
 
• The article "an" is used before words that begin with a vowel sound, whereas "quiet" begins with a consonant sound.
 
• The correct phrase should be "**a quiet street**," ensuring grammatical correctness and clarity.
 
• Thus, the error is located in **Option 3** of the sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 3**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"There’s** a** **quiet street **down the left that you can use for your dance practice."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Option 2: "for your dance practice"** – This part of the sentence is grammatically correct and does not require any changes.
 
• **Option 4: "that you can use"** – This part of the sentence is grammatically correct and does not require any changes.

questions.question:
**Directions: Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error.**

She will come to work though it doesn’t rain tomorrow.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **'though it doesn't'**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In the given sentence, the use of the conjunction 'though' is incorrect.
 
• The conjunction 'though' means **despite the fact that; although**.
 
• The conjunction 'if' should be used in place of 'though'.
 
• The conjunction 'if' is used **for introducing a conditional clause on the condition or supposition that; in the event that**.

Hence, the correct answer is option 4.

Correct Sentence__: *She will come to work **if it doesn’t** rain tomorrow*.

questions.question:
**In the sentence identify the segment which contains the grammatical error.**

The Prime Minister, along with the other ministers have left for America.
questions.solution:
**The correct answer is option 1 i.e. have left**

As a rule, when a sentence refers to 2 subjects, the **verbs in the sentence should refer to the subject that comes first**. Here it is 'the Prime Minister' and he is a singular entity, thus the verbs should also be singular. Thus, **'have' needs to be replaced with 'has'.**

**Thus, the correct answer is option 1. **

questions.question:
Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error.

Mr. Roy was not only very successful and humble also.
questions.solution:
The erroneous part is **'and humble also'**

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__**

__
 
• The given sentence is an example of **correlative conjunction** since it has **not only** in the first clause.
 
• Correlative conjunctions are a **pair of words **that connect **similar entities**(nouns, adjectives, etc) in the sentence **together**.
 
• It is used to put emphasis on certain elements.
 
• Common examples of correlative conjunctions include **either or, neither nor, not only but also, both and**.

**Hence the correct sentence is**__: *Mr. Roy was not only very successful __**but also **__humble*.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

__
 
• Correlative conjunction is also known to maintain the grammatical balance in a sentence.
 
• it can only connect two similar entities together. Like if the first clause of the sentence had a noun then it will be connected to another noun in the second clause of the sentence.
 
 
• Example: **Both** India **and **China have huge populations. (**nouns**)
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/9074044cf96dc1d09ca89eac99180c3d7440ade1b364d09d47931959bf693cc8.png] **Confusion Points__**

 
• It is really easy to get confused about which conjunction to use in a particular sentence.
 
• If the first clause of the statement is similar to the second clause then we can use coordinating conjunction like **and**.
 
 
• **Example**: *He was handsome **and **talented as well*.
 
 
 
• If the first clause of the statement is in stark contrast to the second clause of the statement then we use **but.**
 
 
• **Example: ***He was talented **but **lacked discipline.*
 
 
 
• There is no need to use commas in case two nouns are connected through conjunction but in other sentences a comma is necessary.
 
 
• **Example**: The restaurant owner not only offered us a free lunch, but he also gave us a complimentary beverage.

questions.question:
**Directions: Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error.**

Either Ramesh or Reema have the keys to the cupboard.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**or Reema have**'.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In the given sentence, the **plural form of the verb 'have'** is **incorrect**.
 
• '**Ramesh' and 'Reema' **are **two singular nouns**.
 
• **Two singular nouns connected by 'or' or 'nor' take a singular verb**.
 
• Therefore, the **singular form of the verb 'has' **should be used** in place of the plural verb 'have'**.

Hence, the correct answer is option 4.

Correct Sentence__: *Either Ramesh **or Reema has** the keys to the cupboard*.

questions.question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.

The blue is a beautiful colour.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 1)**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The word 'The' before 'blue' is unnecessary in the context of the given sentence.
 
• In English, we generally do not use the definite article 'the' before colors unless we are referring to something specific that has already been mentioned or is known.
 
• Therefore, the correct sentence should be: ***Blue is a beautiful colour***.

Hence, the correct answer is option 1. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Articles **(a, an, the)** are used before nouns to provide context. **'The'** is a definite article used to refer to something specific.
 
• When talking about colors in a general sense, we do not use the definite article **'the'**.
 
 
• **Example: *****Red** is a vibrant colour.*

questions.question:
Identify the segment in the sentence which contains the grammatical error.

Ram cannot withdraw all his money unless he does not give a prior notice.
questions.solution:
**The correct solution is option 4.**

'unless he does not give' is grammatically incorrect because 'unless' means except if.

Here, 'unless' and 'does not' are contrary to each other. So, it's wrong. 

__Correct sentence__: *Ram cannot withdraw all his money **if** he does not give prior notice.*

* [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__***

 
• “if” is conditional. It is used to describe a possible situation, and what would happen under the conditions of that situation
 
 
• **For E.g.-** "**If **you don't save some money, you can't go on vacation
 
 
 
• “Unless” is also conditional, but it is effectively “if” with an extra exclusion or negative qualifier added
 
 
• **For e.g.-** You can't go on vacation **unless** you save some money.

questions.question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.

She received / an award / for her work / in a engineering field.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '2' i.e. in a engineering field.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The given sentence has been divided into four segments: 
 
 
• **She received**
 
• **an award**
 
• **for her work**
 
• **in a engineering field**
 
 
 
• Segment 2, **"in a engineering field"**, contains a grammatical error.
 
• The article **"a"** is incorrect because it precedes the word **"engineering,"** which begins with a vowel sound. The correct article in this context is **"an."**
 
• The correct phrase should be **"in an engineering field."**

Correct sentence: *She received an award for her work in an engineering field.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Usage of Articles:**
 
 
• **"A":** Used before words that begin with a consonant sound. Example: *a book, a car*.
 
• **"An":** Used before words that begin with a vowel sound. Example: *an apple, an engineer*.
 
 
 
• **Common Errors:**
 
 
• Using the wrong article before a noun can make the sentence grammatically incorrect.
 
• It is important to focus on the **sound** of the word that follows the article, not just the spelling.
 
 
</ul

__
 
• In the given sentence, the use of the plural noun 'publics' and the **plural verb 'are'** is incorrect.
 
• The noun '**public**' is an **uncountable noun or singular noun**.
 
• Therefore, the singular form of the noun 'public' should be used **in place of** the plural form 'publics'.
 
• Also, we know that a **singular noun or subject always takes a singular verb**.
 
• Therefore, the **singular form of the verb 'is'** should be used **in place of** the **plural verb 'are'**.

 

Hence, the correct answer is option 1.

Correct Sentence: *The **public is** not satisfied with the new act*.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Subjects and verbs must agree with one another in number singular or plural.
 
• If a subject is singular, its verb must also be singular; if a subject is a plural, its verb must also be plural.

questions.question:
**Parts of the given sentence have been given as options. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don’t find any error, mark ‘No error’ as your answer.**

Neither she not I am going to take part in the debate competition.
questions.solution:
The erroneous part of the sentence is: **Neither she not I**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• Replace "**not**" with "**nor**" to correct the sentence.
 
• We can use neither as a conjunction with nor. It connects two or more negative alternatives. It is called correlative conjunction.
 
• **Correlative conjunctions** are conjunctions used to illustrate how two words or phrases within a sentence relate to each other.
 
• Correlative conjunctions always come in pairs. (either/or, neither/nor)
 
• '**Neither/nor**' is used when two options are invalid.
 
• In the given sentence it is said that, she and I are not participating in the debate tournament. (both are negative)
 
• We use "**nor**" before the second or farther of two alternatives when "**neither**" introduces the first.

Therefore, the correct answer is **option 3**, which contains the error.

**Corrected sentence:** *Neither she nor I am going to take part in the debate competition.*

• **Articles "a" and "an":**

 
 
• **"A":** Used before words that begin with a consonant sound. Example: a car, a university.
 
• **"An":** Used before words that begin with a vowel sound. Example: an apple, an hour.
 
 
 
• **Common Mistakes:**
 
 
• Incorrect: an university (since "university" starts with a consonant sound).
 
• Correct: a university.

• **'Many' **is countable.__
 __
 
• ​__**Example: ***There are **many **girls in the classroom.*{ here we can count girls }​

• A relative pronoun (“who,” “which,” or “that”) used as a subject of an adjective clause takes either a singular or plural verb in order to agree with its antecedent.

 **Example: **
 
 
• A vegetable that contains DDT can be harmful. (Adjective clause modifying the singular noun “vegetable.”)
 
• Vegetables that contain DDT can be harmful. (Adjective clause modifying the plural noun “vegetables.”)** **
 
 
 
• **​**Here, **'my brother' **is a singular subject, so a singular verb should be used.

**Thus, the rectified sentence is: ***My brother, who** lives** in Delhi, has written me a letter.*

The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains an error.

Neetu have been / waiting for me / since 10 o’clock / in the morning.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is "**Neetu have been.**"

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** 

 
• In the given sentence, the error lies in the first part.
 
• **The subject "Neetu" is singular, but the verb "have been" is plural. **
 
• **This creates a subject-verb agreement error.**
 
• The correct verb form for "Neetu" would be "has been."
 
• The sentence should read: "Neetu has been waiting for me since 10 o'clock in the morning."

Hence, **the correct answer is option 1**.
